tasks.title: CAMP HORIZONS
body: Here are some reviews that parents have written after their kids have been to Camp Horizons.

Christopher Five years in a row attending summer camp at Camp Horizons has consistently led to the first question after picking up my teenage kid: “Can I go again next year?” Communication is great, food is OK, and pricing is good. Even better if you enrol early.

Luke The camp is a great concept, but sadly, if you are not sending your teen camper with friends, they could potentially end up experiencing what mine did: being lonely and laughed at. She also stated that they were forced to clean their cabin daily, and were only allowed 5-minute showers.

Colin The camp portal made filling out the paperwork super easy. It was all very organized, except for the very long check-in line when we dropped our daughter off. The pick-up was super quick and easy though. Huge benefit is the device-free zone.

Eric My son loved his time at camp and even wants to participate in the counsellor program. During his stay I was able to look at pictures that were being taken and shared with the parents. At one point he looked upset in one of the pictures and the counsellors checked up on him for me.

Adam What really makes this camp special is the absolutely amazing staff, who care about kids a lot. The camp also constantly improves each year with new activities, and everything is maintained in top condition. Another pro is that kids are not allowed to have electronics.

Wesley The campsite itself is beautiful with incredible views of the mountains. However, my son was pretty disappointed with the food, even though he did not expect much from “camp-food”. Additionally, the bathrooms and showers were kind of gross. He felt he was leaving a shower feeling dirtier than when he went in.

Zack So disappointing that I trusted my son's summer experience to people that don't deliver what they advertise. They listed 30+ activities to choose from on their website, but in fact, there were only eight options. No wonder the kids missed their devices!

In Portugal's popular seaside town of Albufeira, wearing swimwear off the beach could {{7}}. In Spain's Balearic Islands, public drinking fines can reach €3,000. Hiking Italy's Cinque Terre in inappropriate footwear could see travellers shelling out up to €2,500. France now fines smokers €90 on the spot for {{8}}, and collecting a seashell in Greece could cost €1,000.

At first glance, these measures might seem like {{9}}, since many of these destinations earn a significant amount of money from tourism. But authorities say the rules are aimed at protecting residents and responsible holidaymakers. And while they might sound rigid and punitive, they are all about encouraging responsible and empathetic travelling.

Bad tourism behaviour has gone too far and authorities are trying to protect towns and residents from mass tourism's worst excesses. “Tourism cannot {{10}}. We must act with two main ideas in mind: the protection and preservation of the environment; and {{11}},” said Juan Antonio Amengual, mayor of Calvià, Mallorca.

“Locals are fed up,” said responsible tourism advocate Birgitta Spee-König. “These fines are signals that communities want to {{12}}. Local authorities are recognising that they need to stand up for residents, even if they risk upsetting tourists. It’s also a signal to holidaymakers that being away from home isn’t a free pass for {{13}}.

It's too soon to say if the new fines are working. Behaviour change campaigns {{14}}, and one season won't transform visitor habits. But the message is clear: sun, sand and sea are still on offer, but only to those who agree to enjoy them sensibly, sensitively and a little soberly.

tasks.title: KEEP CALM AND CARRY ON
body: In the spring of 2000, a forgotten World War Two-era British propaganda poster was rediscovered in a dusty box at Barter Books, a second-hand bookshop. The red poster and its bold message beneath a Tudor crown, Keep Calm and Carry On, sparked a viral design trend and became one of the 21st century's most recognisable cultural slogans.

The poster was commissioned in 1939 by the British Ministry of Information, which often used posters, cinema, radio, books and pamphlets to boost public morale during the threat of war. Bombing raids were expected to lead to the rapid breakdown of society, so the poster was designed to help restore order amid the chaos.

British towns and cities did experience heavy bombing raids, but civilians responded with resilience and spirited togetherness. So, the poster would have seemed rather patronising to British civilians. The iconic poster, of which about 2.5 million copies were printed, was held back and remained unseen by the public. Only a few copies survived, including the one in the box at Barter Books.

Stuart and Mary Manley, owners of Barter Books, were taken by the poster. “We decided to have it framed and put it up in the bookshop. We had no idea what it would become.” The explosion began when a Guardian journalist included it in a 2005 article on her 10 favourite design items.

The poster reappeared in a radically different landscape than the one it was intended for, one shaped by a rapidly growing internet culture, and soon became a platform for endless parody. By 2007, sales of the poster had reached 50,000 and its popularity hasn't waned since.

Fuelled by the reach of the internet, the phrase captured the attention of the international media. Today, the message appears on countless T-shirts, mugs, key rings, etc., and since its rediscovery, the poster and its caption have become a meme template and been endlessly reimagined. Keep Calm and Drink Tea. Keep Calm and Code On. Keep Calm and Have a Cupcake. The list goes on.

The poster's plainness is crucial to its adaptability, with the crown at the top, and five large words in white, on a red background: a powerful colour that catches the eye. That's why it is adaptable to contemporary visual culture, where a vast array of media messages compete for our attention.

tasks.title: HOW SHARING A BED WITH YOUR PET AFFECTS YOUR HEALTH
body: Sleeping with pets isn’t a new phenomenon. {{0}} Now that we have heating and locking doors, we no longer need a dog to keep us warm and safe. {{23}}

Pets can bring relief from nightmares for people with post-traumatic stress disorder. Sleeping with them can also provide comfort and reduce anxiety and loneliness. {{24}} Having a pet in your bed can also ease symptoms of mental health conditions and help regulate emotions.

The presence of pets significantly influences the makeup of bacteria found in a home. {{25}} Researchers agree that exposure to a diversity of microorganisms benefits human health and strengthens the immune system.

{{26}} Any of the health benefits of pet contact are likely to disappear if the quality of your sleep is not good enough. For example, your sleep is likely to be disrupted if you have a hyperactive dog in the bed. {{27}}

Cats are more likely to disrupt sleep than dogs, because they’re more active at night. {{28}} On the other hand, dogs also have quirks. They cycle through REM (rapid eye movement) sleep and wakefulness way more often than humans. {{29}}
Pets can also bring saliva, plant components and mold spores into the bed with you. {{30}} Pets might also carry mites, ticks and fleas, which can bite humans and transmit various diseases.

body: Few people welcome the news that they have been sacked and {{0}} come to terms with losing their job. Yet, whether we like it or not, this phrase has been part of the English language for centuries. But where does it come from?

Before the Industrial Revolution – when men, women and even children flocked to factories in search {{1}} work – it was far more common for labourers to move from one job to another. {{2}} than being permanently employed as part of a team, tradesmen, craftsmen, and labourers would travel independently, {{3}} their own tools and materials, and {{4}} employment wherever opportunities arose. The most practical way to transport their equipment was in a sack, which they would {{5}} leave with their employer for safekeeping.

In an age with no job security, formal {{6}}, or trade unions, workers could be dismissed at a moment’s notice. When their {{7}} were no longer required, they were {{8}} their sack – a clear sign that they were to collect their belongings and leave.

tasks.title: THE SOVIET ARTWORK THAT SPIED ON THE US
body: Eighty years ago, during the final weeks of World War II, a troop of {{0}} Pioneers presented the U.S. Ambassador in Moscow with a hand-carved Great Seal of the US at his {{9}} residence called Spaso House. The gift symbolized cooperation between Russia and the U.S. during the war, and the U.S. Ambassador Harriman proudly displayed it in his house.

However, the ambassador and his security team were {{10}} of the seal’s true purpose; it was far more than an ornament. Hidden inside was a listening device, later dubbed “The Thing” by U.S. technical security experts. For seven years, it quietly spied on diplomatic conversations, its {{11}} never suspected. By using a seemingly {{12}} artwork to infiltrate the enemy, the Soviets accomplished the most ingenious stunt since Odysseus's Trojan Horse.

Within Spaso House, The Thing was only activated when a remote transceiver, based in a nearby building, was switched on. This sent out a high-frequency signal, which reflected the vibrations coming from the bug's antenna. Its {{13}} came to light in 1951, when a British military radio {{14}} working in Moscow accidentally tuned into the precise wavelength used by The Thing and overheard conversations from a {{15}} room. The following year, U.S. technicians swept the ambassadorial residence and, after no fewer than three days of searching, realized that the hand-carved Great Seal was an {{16}} ear, eavesdropping on behind-the-scenes ambassadorial discussions.

tasks.title: WHAT GOES AROUND COMES AROUND
body: Common Courtesy Day, celebrated on 21 March, serves {{0}} a reminder of the simple behaviors that help keep society from descending into chaos. It also raises awareness of {{17}} valuable courtesy is in everyday life and encourages people to practice it more consciously. Although the exact origin of the day is still unknown, it is believed to {{18}} started around 2003.

Common courtesy can be expressed through simple actions, {{19}} as saying “please” and “thank you” when asking for or receiving help or a service. Small gestures – like letting someone go ahead in traffic, holding the door for another person, or offering to help with groceries – can have a lasting impact. You might also give up your seat on public transport to someone who needs it more.

If courtesy is {{20}} yet part of your everyday life, Common Courtesy Day is the perfect opportunity to make a change. Try to use polite words more often and acknowledge the kindness of others. Not {{21}} will others appreciate it, but you will feel good about it as well.

You might wonder {{22}} there is such a thing as “uncommon courtesy”. In a sense, the answer is yes. Since common courtesy has become less common, acts of politeness can now stand out more than ever. In the past, for example, people often stood up when someone entered a room, {{23}} was considered standard manners. While this custom has fallen out of fashion, those who still practice it demonstrate {{24}} could be called uncommon courtesy – going beyond everyday politeness.
